title: Consent as a defence
subtitle: Where the victim's agreement does, and does not, excuse harm
objectives: State the general rule that consent is not a defence to actual bodily harm or worse, and identify the recognised public interest exceptions
Explain how R v Brown and R v Wilson mark the contested boundary of consent to bodily harm, including in a sexual or intimate context
Apply the informed-consent principle from R v Dica and the statutory bar in s 71 Domestic Abuse Act 2021 to new fact patterns

leadingAuthorities.role: General rule: consent is no defence to actual bodily harm or worse without a recognised public interest exception
House of Lords refuses to extend the exceptions to consensual harm inflicted for sexual gratification
Treats consensual branding between spouses as analogous to tattooing, a recognised exception
Consent to sexual intercourse is not consent to the risk of disease transmission unless that risk is informed
Statutory bar: consent to serious harm for sexual gratification is no defence where death results

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Consent looks like a simple word until you have to say exactly where it stops working as a defence. Where the profile shows students tend to state the general rule confidently but struggle to place new facts against the exceptions, this brief note appears: 'You know consent has limits — this lesson is about naming exactly where they sit.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well recalling the rule and the case names before. The test pool below leans hard on fact patterns: expect to place a scenario against Brown, Wilson or Dica rather than just recite them.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Slow down on Parts 1 and 2 and get the general rule and the list of exceptions solid before moving on — the rest of the lesson assumes you can state both without prompting.

overview.hook: Two people agree, in advance, to something that leaves one of them injured. Sometimes the law shrugs — a boxing match, a tattoo, a surgeon's scalpel. Sometimes it doesn't care what was agreed at all. The difference isn't how much harm was done, or even how freely it was chosen. It's a line Parliament and the courts have drawn, redrawn, and argued over for decades — and this lesson is about learning exactly where it currently sits.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 22 September 2026. The statutory bar in s 71 Domestic Abuse Act 2021 is a comparatively recent addition to a common-law area that remains actively contested; watch for further appellate comment on its interaction with R v Wilson.

parts.heading: The baseline: your consent doesn't reach that far
body: Start with the rule as the courts actually state it, not the softened version students often carry into exams. Consent is a full defence to common assault and to battery involving no injury or only trifling harm. The moment the injury reaches the threshold of actual bodily harm — under s 47 Offences Against the Person Act 1861 — or anything more serious, consent alone stops being enough.

That threshold was confirmed in A-G's Reference (No 6 of 1980), a case about two teenagers who agreed to settle an argument with a fist fight and where one of them ended up with a bloody nose and bruising. The Court of Appeal held that it is not in the public interest for people to cause each other actual bodily harm for no good reason, and that consent between the parties does not, by itself, provide one.

Notice what that reasoning is actually protecting. It isn't primarily the victim, who has already agreed. It's a broader public interest in limiting violence generally — which is why the defence doesn't turn on how genuinely or freely the victim consented, but on whether the activity itself falls within a recognised category the law is prepared to tolerate. Sport, surgery, tattooing, and a handful of others qualify. Ordinary fighting does not, however sporting the intent.

components.definition: A recognised category of activity (such as properly conducted sport, surgery, or tattooing) in which the law permits consent to operate as a defence even to actual bodily harm or worse, because the activity itself is treated as socially useful or tolerable — the exception is to the category of conduct, not to the individual case.

interaction.prompt: Two colleagues agree, entirely voluntarily, to settle a dispute with a bare-knuckle fight in a car park. One suffers a fractured cheekbone. Is the other's consent a defence to a charge of actual bodily harm?
options: No — an ordinary fight is not a recognised public interest exception, however genuine the consent
Yes — genuine, informed consent between adults is always a complete defence
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. A-G's Reference (No 6 of 1980) is precisely this fact pattern: genuine consent, real injury, no recognised exception — and no defence.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — the strength or genuineness of the consent isn't the test here. The question is whether the activity falls within a recognised exception, and an ordinary fist fight does not.

parts.heading: R v Brown: consent meets its limit
body: A group of men, all consenting adults, engaged in private sadomasochistic activity over a period of years that caused each other injury — nothing life-threatening or requiring hospital treatment, but more than trifling. Nothing about the encounters was non-consensual; nothing was reported by any participant. The prosecution came to light through an unrelated police investigation, and the men were charged under ss 47 and 20 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861.

The case reached the House of Lords, and by a narrow 3–2 majority, their Lordships held that consent was no defence. The activity did not fall within any recognised exception, and the majority declined to create a new one for consensual injury inflicted for sexual gratification — reasoning that the public interest in discouraging the deliberate infliction of injury outweighed the men's interest in private sexual autonomy, and that extending the exceptions was, in any event, a matter better left to Parliament than to the courts.

The recognised exceptions, as the House of Lords confirmed them, remain a fairly short and specific list: properly conducted sport, reasonable surgical intervention, tattooing and ear or body piercing performed with consent, religious mortification in limited circumstances, and rough horseplay between friends that goes wrong without intent to injure. Brown itself does not fall within any of these — and the majority's refusal to extend the list is the core of the case's continuing controversy, discussed further in the next part.

components.factsShort: Consenting adults caused each other actual bodily harm and wounding in private, for sexual gratification; convictions under ss 47 and 20 OAPA 1861 were upheld.
components.ratioShort: Consent is not a defence to actual bodily harm or wounding inflicted for sexual gratification; the recognised public interest exceptions are not extended to cover it.

expanded.facts: The defendants were a group of adult men who, over several years and entirely in private, engaged in consensual sadomasochistic activity that caused each other injury, including bruising and minor wounding, none requiring medical treatment. No participant complained; the prosecution arose from a separate police investigation.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The majority held that the public interest requires that a line be drawn between what the law will and will not tolerate, and that deliberately inflicting injury for the pleasure the infliction itself provides falls on the wrong side of that line regardless of consent. The dissenting Lords argued this intruded into private sexual conduct between adults that caused no lasting harm and no complaint from any participant.
expanded.significance: Brown remains the leading authority that consent, however genuine, does not extend the categories of lawful harm beyond those the courts and Parliament have already recognised — and that the courts will not create a new exception simply because the harm was sexual and consensual.

components.label: Recognised public interest exceptions
points: Properly conducted sport, played within its rules
Tattooing and ear or body piercing carried out with consent
Rough and undisciplined horseplay between friends, where there is no intent to injure

interaction.prompt: Which of these is a recognised public interest exception to the general rule that consent is no defence to actual bodily harm?
options: Consensual injury inflicted purely for the sexual gratification it provides
A properly conducted contact sport played within its rules
Any injury the participants agreed to in advance, regardless of context
interaction.trapExplanation: The other two options both describe 'genuine consent' as if it were the test — but Brown decided precisely that genuine, private, consensual sexual activity causing injury is not automatically an exception. Only the specific recognised categories qualify.

parts.heading: Wilson and the shifting exception
body: Here's a question worth sitting with before the answer is given: a husband, at his wife's request, uses a hot knife to brand his initials onto her buttocks. She later needs medical treatment and, in the course of that treatment, the injury comes to a doctor's attention, who reports it. Is this closer to Brown — consensual infliction of injury for gratification, no defence — or closer to tattooing, a recognised exception?

The Court of Appeal in R v Wilson went with the latter. It treated what had happened as analogous to tattooing — a form of personal adornment carried out with consent, within a marriage, that the criminal law had no legitimate business prosecuting. The court was explicit that this was not a proper matter for criminal prosecution at all, and quashed the conviction.

So did Wilson quietly narrow Brown, or carve out a genuinely separate category? The honest answer is that the law has never fully resolved this. Wilson emphasised the marital context and the analogy to tattooing; it did not purport to overrule Brown, and the House of Lords in Brown had already been clear that tattooing itself is an exception. But commentators have long noted the discomfort in the pairing: an activity involving comparable pain and a comparable branding-with-a-blade element to Brown's facts was treated as lawful, while Brown's was not — and the difference in outcome tracked, uncomfortably, a difference in the sexual and social context of who was asking.

What you should take from this is not a confident rule that resolves every new fact pattern, but an accurate map of where the boundary is genuinely unsettled — because that unsettled boundary is exactly what an examiner will test.

components.factsShort: A husband branded his initials onto his wife's skin with a hot knife, at her request; the Court of Appeal treated this as analogous to tattooing and quashed the resulting conviction.
components.ratioShort: Consensual branding within a marriage, analogous to tattooing, falls within a recognised exception and is not a proper matter for criminal prosecution.

expanded.facts: Alan Wilson branded his initials onto his wife Sharon's buttocks using a hot knife, at her request and in the privacy of their home. The act came to medical attention only because she later required treatment for the resulting burn. Wilson was convicted of actual bodily harm at trial.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held that consensual activity between husband and wife, in the privacy of the matrimonial home, was not a proper matter for criminal investigation or prosecution, and drew an analogy with the recognised exception for tattooing.
expanded.significance: Wilson shows the exceptions are not a closed, mechanically applied list — courts have some latitude to reason by analogy. It also illustrates why students should treat the Brown/Wilson boundary as contested rather than settled: the two cases are difficult to reconcile on principle alone.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often state that Wilson overruled or reversed Brown.
components.whyItsWrong: Wilson did not purport to overrule Brown and could not have done so from the Court of Appeal in any event. It reasoned by analogy to the tattooing exception that Brown itself had already recognised — it narrowed the practical application at the margins without disturbing Brown's core holding.

interaction.prompt: Which scenario is the Court of Appeal in Wilson most concerned with distinguishing from Brown?
interaction.scenarioA: A group of acquaintances, meeting for that purpose, deliberately inflict injury on each other for the pleasure the pain itself provides.
interaction.scenarioB: A spouse brands their partner's skin at the partner's request, in private, in a manner the court treats as comparable to a tattoo.
interaction.explanation: Scenario B is Wilson's own facts — reasoned as analogous to a recognised exception (tattooing) rather than as an extension of Brown's refusal to recognise sadomasochistic injury as an exception in itself.

parts.heading: Consent to sex is not consent to infection: R v Dica
body: A different kind of consent problem: what happens when someone consents to sexual intercourse without knowing their partner is HIV-positive, and is later infected? Mohammed Dica was charged under s 20 OAPA 1861 — inflicting grievous bodily harm — after two complainants contracted HIV following unprotected sex with him, without having been told of his status.

The Court of Appeal held that consenting to sexual intercourse is not, without more, consent to the risk of contracting a serious disease. What matters is whether the complainant's consent was informed — if she knew of the defendant's HIV status and freely chose to run the risk anyway, that consent could found a defence. Where the risk was concealed, there was no true consent to it, and liability could follow.

This is a structurally different move from Brown. Brown holds that consent is barred as a matter of public policy regardless of how informed or genuine it was — the category of harm is simply excluded. Dica holds instead that consent can operate normally as a defence to this kind of harm, provided it meets an ordinary standard of being informed — the problem in Dica's own case was the absence of disclosure, not a policy bar on the defence existing at all.

Keep these two principles distinct. An exam question that asks you to apply 'informed consent' reasoning to a Brown-style fact pattern, or a public-policy bar to a Dica-style one, has confused the two doctrines — and that confusion is exactly what the test items below are designed to catch.

components.label: Informed consent: the structure
points: Consent to intercourse does not automatically include consent to the risk of disease transmission
Consent to that specific risk must be established separately, and must be informed
Where the defendant conceals a known infection risk, the complainant's consent to intercourse does not extend to the risk of transmission
Where the complainant knows the risk and freely chooses to proceed anyway, informed consent can operate as a defence

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that determines whether the complainant's consent extends to the risk of infection in this scenario.
interaction.scenarioText: Farid knows he has an active, transmissible infection. He and a new partner have unprotected sex. He does not mention his diagnosis at any point, and his partner later tests positive for the same infection.
tappableSpans: knows he has an active, transmissible infection
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The infection itself and the act of sex are not what decide the case — it's the concealment. Consent to sex was given, but not informed consent to this specific risk, because the risk was never disclosed.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at what would change the outcome if it were different. Farid having the infection and having unprotected sex are both constants here — the disclosure (or its absence) is what determines whether consent to the risk existed at all.

parts.heading: Parliament closes a door: the s 71 bar
body: For years, a small but recurring pattern of cases saw defendants argue, in response to a partner's death during sexual activity, that the deceased had consented to violent conduct as part of that activity — sometimes called, in media shorthand, the 'rough sex defence'. Whatever the individual merits of any one such argument, the pattern itself became a matter of public and parliamentary concern, not least because it risked functioning as a route around Brown's own bar on consent to serious injury, by reframing the same conduct as something a jury might be persuaded to treat differently when a death, rather than a survivable injury, was the result.

Parliament responded directly. Section 71 of the Domestic Abuse Act 2021 provides that, where a person suffers serious harm and the defendant caused it, it is not a defence that the person consented to the infliction of that harm for the purposes of obtaining sexual gratification. The provision places beyond doubt — as a matter of statute rather than judicial discretion case by case — that consent cannot excuse serious harm inflicted in this context.

There's a case for reading s 71 as simply Brown restated in statutory language for a specific, high-stakes context: Parliament codifying what the House of Lords had already held in principle, so that no future court could be tempted to treat a death case differently from an injury case. There's also a harder question the statute doesn't fully resolve — how it sits alongside Wilson's more permissive reasoning about consensual harm between intimate partners outside the abuse context. That tension is unresolved, and worth naming rather than glossing over: s 71 targets serious harm caused for sexual gratification specifically, and doesn't purport to reopen or settle the Wilson-style boundary discussed earlier in this lesson.

Handle this material precisely rather than sensationally in any answer you write. The doctrinal point examiners are testing is narrow and statutory: consent is not a defence to serious harm inflicted for sexual gratification, by force of s 71, independent of whatever the common law says elsewhere.

components.text: If a person ('D') is charged with an offence listed in subsection (3) in respect of anything done to another person ('V'), it is not a defence that V consented to the infliction of the harm that D caused, or intended to cause, V for the purposes of obtaining sexual gratification.
elements: D causes or intends to cause serious harm to V
The harm is inflicted for the purposes of obtaining sexual gratification
V's consent to the infliction of that harm is not a defence

interaction.prompt: Under s 71 Domestic Abuse Act 2021, which element must be established before the consent bar applies?
options: That the harm was inflicted for the purposes of obtaining sexual gratification
That the defendant and complainant were married or in a long-term relationship
That the complainant reported the harm to the police at the time
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — s 71 is targeted specifically at harm caused for sexual gratification. Relationship status and reporting are not elements of the provision.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Re-read the statutory text. The provision is defined by the purpose behind the harm — sexual gratification — not by the relationship between the parties or by whether the incident was reported.

testPool.prompt: State the general rule on consent as a defence to actual bodily harm or worse.
acceptableAnswers: consent is no defence to actual bodily harm or worse without a recognised exception
no defence to ABH or above absent a public interest exception
testPool.modelAnswer: Consent is a defence to assault and to battery causing no or trifling harm, but it is not, by itself, a defence to actual bodily harm or anything more serious, unless the activity falls within a recognised public interest exception.

testPool.prompt: In R v Brown, did the House of Lords create a new exception covering consensual harm inflicted for sexual gratification?
options: No — the majority declined to extend the recognised exceptions to cover it
Yes — a new exception for private, consensual sexual activity was recognised

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT among the recognised public interest exceptions confirmed in Brown?
options: Properly conducted sport
Reasonable surgical intervention
Consensual injury inflicted for sexual gratification
Tattooing carried out with consent
testPool.trapExplanation: This is the very category Brown refused to recognise as an exception. It reads plausibly alongside the genuine exceptions, which is exactly why it's the trap.

testPool.prompt: Order the reasoning steps a court follows when a defendant raises consent to a charge of actual bodily harm or worse.
items: Identify the level of harm caused
If the harm is no more than trifling, consent is a full defence
If the harm is actual bodily harm or worse, ask whether the activity falls within a recognised public interest exception
If no recognised exception applies, consent is not a defence regardless of how genuine it was

testPool.prompt: Section 71 Domestic Abuse Act 2021 bars consent as a defence in relation to which specific type of harm?
options: Serious harm caused for the purposes of obtaining sexual gratification
Any harm caused during a domestic dispute
Harm caused during a properly conducted contact sport

testPool.prompt: In the passage below adapted from R v Dica, highlight the sentence that states the informed-consent principle.
testPool.passage: The complainants had consented to sexual intercourse with the defendant. However, consent to intercourse itself is not the same as consent to the risk of contracting a serious disease. Where a complainant is unaware of an infection risk that the defendant knows about and conceals, the complainant's consent does not extend to that risk, and the defendant is not thereby excused.
testPool.ratioSentence: Where a complainant is unaware of an infection risk that the defendant knows about and conceals, the complainant's consent does not extend to that risk, and the defendant is not thereby excused.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that R v Wilson formally overruled R v Brown?
testPool.explanation: Wilson reasoned by analogy to the tattooing exception Brown itself had already recognised. It did not, and as a Court of Appeal decision could not, overrule a House of Lords authority — the two sit uneasily together rather than one displacing the other.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that most strongly supports treating this scenario as analogous to Wilson rather than to Brown.
testPool.scenarioText: A tattoo artist, working from a licensed studio and following standard hygiene practice, tattoos a client's arm at the client's request, causing the ordinary bruising and skin damage tattooing involves.
testPool.explanation: Tattooing is itself a named exception, independent of hygiene practice or licensing — the operative fact is that this is tattooing carried out with the client's consent, which places it squarely within the recognised category regardless of the studio's conditions.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario more closely mirrors the reasoning in R v Dica rather than R v Brown?
testPool.scenarioA: A defendant knowingly conceals a transmissible infection from a sexual partner, who later tests positive.
testPool.scenarioB: A group of friends deliberately inflict injury on each other purely for the pleasure the infliction itself provides, entirely in private.
testPool.explanation: Scenario A turns on whether consent was informed — the Dica question. Scenario B is barred by public policy regardless of how informed or genuine the consent was, which is the Brown question.

testPool.prompt: During a properly refereed rugby match, a tackle within the rules causes a broken collarbone. Does the injured player's participation in the match provide a defence to a charge of actual bodily harm?
options: Yes — properly conducted sport, played within its rules, is a recognised exception
No — any injury above trifling harm defeats consent regardless of context
Only if the injured player signed a written waiver beforehand
testPool.explanation: Sport played within its rules is one of the named exceptions confirmed in Brown. A written waiver is not required — the exception attaches to the nature of the activity itself.

testPool.prompt: Priya tells a new partner about her diagnosed transmissible infection before they have unprotected sex. He says he understands the risk and wants to proceed anyway. He later contracts the infection. Applying Dica, has Priya's partner given informed consent to that risk?
options: Yes — he was told of the risk and freely chose to proceed regardless
No — informed consent to a health risk is never legally effective
testPool.explanation: Dica draws the line at disclosure. Once the risk is genuinely disclosed and the partner freely chooses to run it, that consent can operate as a defence — unlike Brown, informed consent here is not barred as a matter of policy.

testPool.prompt: A defendant is charged in connection with serious harm caused to a partner, and argues the partner consented to the conduct for the purposes of sexual gratification. Does s 71 Domestic Abuse Act 2021 allow that consent to operate as a defence?
options: No — s 71 expressly bars consent as a defence in these circumstances
Yes — provided the consent was clear and freely given

testPool.prompt: Two experienced amateur boxers agree to a bout outside any sanctioned competition, with no referee and no medical staff present, 'just to settle things'. One suffers a broken nose. Analyse whether consent provides a defence to a charge of actual bodily harm.
factsToOrder: The bout is not part of any sanctioned competition
There is no referee and no medical staff present
One party suffers a broken nose
The stated purpose was to 'settle things', not to compete in the sport

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the parties' agreement to fight provides a defence to a charge of actual bodily harm, given the injury exceeds trifling harm.
modelAnswer.rule: Consent is not a defence to actual bodily harm or worse unless the activity falls within a recognised public interest exception, such as properly conducted sport played within its rules (A-G's Reference (No 6 of 1980); R v Brown).
modelAnswer.application: The sporting exception exists for properly conducted sport, played within its rules — the structure that makes boxing tolerable is precisely the refereeing, medical oversight and rule-following absent here. An unsanctioned, unrefereed bout undertaken to 'settle things' looks structurally more like the ordinary fight in A-G's Reference than like a properly conducted sporting contest, despite both parties being experienced boxers and both freely agreeing.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Consent is unlikely to provide a defence: the activity does not fall within the sporting exception as recognised, because it lacks the features (sanctioning, oversight, rules being followed) that justify that exception existing at all.

testPool.prompt: Which statement most accurately describes the relationship between R v Brown and R v Wilson?
options: Wilson overruled Brown and consent is now generally a defence to consensual sexual harm
Wilson reasoned by analogy to the existing tattooing exception on its own specific facts, without disturbing Brown's refusal to create a general exception for harm inflicted for sexual gratification
Brown and Wilson concern entirely unrelated areas of law and have no bearing on each other
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answer treats Wilson as a reversal of Brown because the outcomes differ. But Wilson's reasoning is narrower and case-specific — an analogy to a pre-existing exception — not a rejection of Brown's core principle.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is collapsing two different doctrines into one: treating Brown's public-policy bar (consent barred regardless of how informed it was) as if it were the same question as Dica's informed-consent test (consent can be a defence, if properly informed). Keep asking which doctrine a fact pattern is actually testing before reaching for an answer.
